set.detail: Born Gaius Octavius on 23 September 63 BC in Rome, son of a new man from Velitrae and of Atia, Julius Caesar's niece, Octavian was adopted in Caesar's will in 44 BC and, at nineteen, raised a private army, fought Antony at Mutina, formed the triumvirate with Antony and Lepidus, proscribed his enemies, defeated the Liberators at Philippi, besieged Perusia, crushed Sextus Pompey and finally defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium (31 BC). The settlements of 27 and 23 BC turned his military supremacy into a lasting constitutional form: a provincial command over most legions, tribunician power and maius imperium, dressed in the language of a restored Republic and the informal title princeps. Over a 41-year reign he created the standing army with fixed terms and a military treasury, the praetorian guard, urban cohorts and vigiles, a provincial administration of legates and equestrian prefects and procurators, the cura annonae, the regions and vici of Rome and the imperial cult. He transformed the city, claiming to have found it brick and left it marble, and promoted a programme of moral and religious renewal through the marriage laws, the Secular Games of 17 BC and the restoration of 82 temples. His wars added Egypt, north-west Spain, the Alps, Noricum, Raetia, Pannonia, Galatia, Moesia and Judaea, but the Illyrian revolt and the loss of Varus's legions ended expansion in Germany. His great weakness was the succession: Marcellus, Agrippa, Gaius and Lucius died before him, and he was forced to adopt Tiberius. His private life was simple: he lived in a modest house on the Palatine, wore clothes woven by his household, suffered chronic illness and gambled at dice. The ancient verdict was divided: Tacitus (Annals 1.9-10) sets the praise of admirers against the critics who saw only deceit, cruelty and a lust for power. Modern interpretations range from Syme's cold revolutionary to Galinsky's cultural visionary. He died at Nola on 19 August AD 14 and was deified.

Livia Drusilla, born on 30 January 58 BC, daughter of Marcus Livius Drusus Claudianus, who killed himself after Philippi, married her cousin Tiberius Claudius Nero and bore him Tiberius (42 BC). After fleeing with him through Sicily and Greece in the civil wars, she was divorced in 39 BC and married Octavian on 17 January 38 BC while six months pregnant with Drusus, a union that brought Octavian the prestige of the Claudii and lasted 52 years without children. She played the role of the virtuous Roman matron and was the first woman to receive the sacrosanctity of a tribune (35 BC), statues and, in 9 BC after Drusus's death, the ius trium liberorum. She owned vast estates and workshops across the empire, managed a household of over a thousand slaves and freedmen known from the columbarium of her familia, and acted as patron to client kings, Herod's family, provincial cities and senatorial families, including Otho's grandfather and Galba. Her villa at Prima Porta, ad gallinas albas, with its painted garden room and the statue of Augustus, and her house on the Palatine survive. Augustus consulted her on policy and Dio credits her with persuading him to pardon Cinna. By his will she was adopted into the Julian family as Julia Augusta. Under Tiberius, her influence and her claims to share in decisions created tension; Tiberius refused the Senate's proposals to call him "son of Julia" or give her the title mater patriae. She died in 29 aged 86, and Tiberius did not attend her funeral or execute her will; Caligula, who called her "Ulysses in a stola", delivered the eulogy. Claudius deified her in 42. The hostile tradition, especially Tacitus and Dio, accused her of poisoning Marcellus, Gaius, Lucius, Agrippa Postumus, Germanicus and even Augustus to advance Tiberius, charges with no solid basis that reflect hostility to female power. Modern biographers (Barrett) stress her political skill and her model of the imperial woman as dynastic mediator.

Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, born c. 63 BC of obscure family, studied with Octavian at Apollonia and was with him when news of Caesar's murder arrived; he remained his closest collaborator for thirty years. He prosecuted Cassius in absentia, commanded at Perusia, as governor of Gaul crossed the Rhine (39-38 BC) and resettled the Ubii, and as consul in 37 BC built the Portus Julius in the Lucrine lake to train a fleet with which he defeated Sextus Pompey at Mylae and Naulochus (36 BC), earning the naval crown. His command of the left wing at Actium won the decisive battle. As aedile in 33 BC, after holding the consulship, he renovated Rome's water supply and sewers, distributing oil and salt and providing free baths and barbers. He was consul again in 28 and 27 BC with Octavian and conducted the census. After 23 BC he received a maius imperium in the East and tribunician power in 18 BC, renewed in 13, and married Julia (21 BC), siring Gaius, Lucius, Julia, Agrippina and Agrippa Postumus. He completed the Cantabrian war in 19 BC with severe measures against his own mutinous troops, settled the Bosporus in 14 BC, befriended Herod, and was commissioned to pacify Pannonia shortly before his death in 12 BC. His buildings included the Pantheon, the Baths of Agrippa, the Saepta Julia, the Aqua Virgo and Aqua Julia, and his geographical commentaries underpinned the map displayed in the Porticus Vipsania. He refused triumphs offered to him, setting a precedent that later restricted triumphs to the imperial family. Seneca the Elder reports that aristocrats despised his origins, and Agrippa himself suppressed his gentile name Vipsanius. Pliny records he suffered painful gout in his last years. His grandchildren included Caligula and Agrippina the Younger, and his great-grandson was Nero. Tacitus and Dio portray him as the indispensable loyal partner, and modern historians agree that the Principate would hardly have been possible without him.

Gaius Maecenas, born c. 70 BC at Arretium of an Etruscan royal line (Horace calls him "descended from kings"), remained an equestrian all his life and never held a magistracy, yet was Octavian's chief political agent in the triumviral years. He negotiated the marriage of Octavian and Scribonia (40 BC), helped broker the treaties of Brundisium (40 BC) and Tarentum (37 BC) with Antony, and governed Rome and Italy informally during Octavian's absences, notably during the Actium campaign, when he suppressed the conspiracy of the younger Lepidus (30 BC). His greatest legacy was cultural patronage: from about 39 BC he supported Virgil, who dedicated the Georgics to him, Horace, to whom he gave the Sabine farm, Propertius and Varius, so that his name became the generic word for a patron of the arts. Through his circle the poets helped articulate the ideology of the new regime without crude propaganda. Maecenas was famous for luxury and effeminacy: he wore loose tunics, loved gems and silks, was the first to build a heated swimming pool in Rome, and wrote mannered prose and verse that Augustus parodied and Seneca condemned. His gardens on the Esquiline, built over a paupers' cemetery, were famous. His influence waned after 23 BC, when his wife Terentia's brother Licinius Murena was implicated in a conspiracy and Maecenas warned her, angering Augustus; there were also rumours of Augustus's affair with Terentia. Seneca, who disliked him, reports that he suffered from insomnia and listened to distant music to fall asleep, and quotes his verses expressing a desperate wish to live even maimed. He died in 8 BC, leaving his estate to Augustus and asking him to "remember Horace as you would myself". Dio gives him a long speech advising Octavian to establish a monarchy (52.14-40), a third-century composition. Modern scholars debate how far Maecenas directed the poets as opposed to providing a framework of patronage.

Julia, born in 39 BC, was Augustus's only child, by his second wife Scribonia, whom he divorced on the day of her birth. Raised strictly under Livia's supervision, taught to spin and weave and forbidden to speak to anyone without permission, she became the key instrument of her father's dynastic policy. She married her cousin Marcellus (25 BC), then Agrippa (21 BC), with whom she had five children, travelled with him in the East, where cities honoured her as a goddess, and after his death was married to Tiberius (11 BC), who had to divorce Vipsania. The marriage failed, and their only child died in infancy. Julia was intelligent, witty and popular; Macrobius preserves her sayings, such as her retort, when asked how her children resembled Agrippa despite her affairs, that she only took on passengers when the ship was full. In 2 BC, the year of the Forum of Augustus and the title pater patriae, Augustus learned of her adulteries and, without consulting her, denounced her in a letter to the Senate, banishing her to the island of Pandateria. Her lovers allegedly included Iullus Antonius, son of Mark Antony, who was executed or committed suicide, and other nobles such as Sempronius Gracchus and Quinctius Crispinus, who were exiled. Augustus refused all appeals, saying that she should have such a daughter and wife, and after five years allowed her to move to Rhegium, but she was never permitted wine, luxuries or visitors without his inspection. When Tiberius became emperor he cut her allowance, and she died of starvation or despair in 14. Augustus excluded her from his Mausoleum. Ancient writers saw a moral scandal; many modern historians suspect that the affair concealed a political conspiracy around Iullus Antonius and her son-in-law Paullus Aemilius, perhaps aimed at Tiberius or at securing power for her sons, as the severity of the punishment suggests.
set.debate: Moral scandal or political conspiracy behind her exile.

set.detail: Nero Claudius Drusus, born in January 38 BC, three months after Livia married Octavian, was raised in Augustus's household with his elder brother Tiberius and became the most popular member of the family. With Tiberius he conquered the Raeti and Vindelici in 15 BC, crossing the Alps from Italy while Tiberius advanced from Gaul. As governor of the Three Gauls from 13 BC he dedicated the Altar of Rome and Augustus at Lugdunum on 1 August 12 BC, the day Claudius was born there. In four campaigns from 12 to 9 BC he invaded Germany: he dug the canal from the Rhine to the IJssel, sailed along the North Sea coast and won over the Frisii, defeated the Sugambri, Usipetes and Bructeri, fought the Chatti and Cherusci, nearly lost his army in an ambush at Arbalo (11 BC), built forts at Aliso and on the Taunus, and in 9 BC reached the Elbe, where, Dio says, a giant barbarian woman appeared and warned him to turn back. On the return march he fell from his horse and broke his leg, dying after thirty days of gangrene in his summer camp; Tiberius rode 200 miles in a day and night to reach his deathbed. His body was carried to Rome, the soldiers erected a cenotaph at Mogontiacum, where an annual festival was held, and he was given the posthumous name Germanicus, inherited by his son. Augustus delivered a eulogy and composed his epitaph. Suetonius and Tacitus report that Drusus favoured restoring the Republic and had written to Tiberius suggesting they force Augustus to do so, which later fuelled rumours that Augustus poisoned him, which modern scholars reject. He married Antonia Minor, by whom he had Germanicus, Livilla and Claudius. The Consolatio ad Liviam, a poem on his death attributed to Ovid, and the Tropaeum in Mainz (the Drususstein) commemorate him. His campaigns brought Germany between Rhine and Elbe under Roman control for nearly two decades.

Tiberius Claudius Nero, born on 16 November 42 BC, son of Tiberius Claudius Nero and Livia, became Augustus's stepson when his mother remarried in 38 BC. As a teenager he delivered his father's eulogy, rode in the Actium triumph and served in the Cantabrian war. In 20 BC he received the Parthian standards and crowned Tigranes in Armenia; with Drusus he conquered the Alpine peoples (15 BC); he subdued Pannonia (12-9 BC) and, after Drusus's death, Germany, deporting 40,000 Sugambri. Forced to divorce Vipsania and marry Julia, and overshadowed by Gaius and Lucius, he withdrew to Rhodes in 6 BC for seven years. Recalled and adopted in AD 4, he campaigned in Germany, crushed the Illyrian revolt (6-9) and stabilised the Rhine after Varus. Emperor at 55 in 14, he ruled conscientiously for 23 years: he refused divine honours and titles, deferred to the Senate, kept provincial governors in post for long periods ("a good shepherd shears his flock, does not flay it"), avoided wars and new conquests, balanced the budget and left a surplus of 2.7 billion sesterces. But his reserve and dissimulation alienated the aristocracy; the death of Germanicus, the destruction of Agrippina's family and the expanding use of maiestas trials created a climate of fear. From 26 he lived on Capri and let Sejanus rule Rome until his fall in 31, after which the treason trials intensified. Suetonius's stories of depravity on Capri, with swimming boys called his "minnows", are generally discounted as hostile gossip. He died at Misenum in 37, possibly hastened by Macro, and was not deified. Tacitus's portrait of a hypocrite whose true nature was gradually revealed is a literary masterpiece but has been challenged by modern historians (Levick, Seager), who see a capable but awkward aristocrat ill-suited to the role of popular princeps, whose administration was among the most competent of the period. Velleius's panegyric offers the contemporary official view.

Germanicus Julius Caesar, born on 24 May 15 BC as son of Drusus the Elder and Antonia Minor, took his father's posthumous cognomen and was adopted by Tiberius in AD 4 at Augustus's command, marrying Augustus's granddaughter Agrippina the Elder, by whom he had nine children, including Caligula and Agrippina the Younger. He served in the Illyrian war and on the Rhine, was consul in 12 and in 13 received command of the eight legions on the Rhine. When the legions mutinied on Augustus's death in 14 and offered him the throne, he refused, threatening to kill himself, and restored order by sending away his wife and infant son Gaius ("Little Boots"), the soldiers' favourite. In three campaigns (14-16) he attacked the Marsi, Chatti, Bructeri and Cherusci, buried the remains of Varus's legions, recovered two eagles and defeated Arminius at Idistaviso and the Angrivarian wall, but suffered heavy losses, including the shipwreck of 16. Tiberius recalled him, granted him a triumph (26 May 17) and sent him east with maius imperium, where he settled Armenia, Cappadocia and Commagene. His unauthorised visit to Egypt, Tiberius's private domain, and his quarrels with Piso preceded his death near Antioch in October 19. He was a talented orator and wrote Greek comedies and a Latin translation of Aratus's astronomical poem Phaenomena, which survives. Tacitus presents him as the ideal Roman prince, a contrast to Tiberius and a lost hope of a gentler principate, comparing him to Alexander the Great, but also notes his rashness and theatricality. Modern historians are more critical of his German campaigns, which achieved little at great cost, and his flamboyance. His popularity made his family the focus of opposition to Tiberius and Sejanus and later secured the throne for his son Caligula, his brother Claudius and his grandson Nero. The honours voted after his death, known from the Tabula Siarensis and Hebana, show the cult of his memory.

Vipsania Agrippina, born c. 14 BC, daughter of Agrippa and Julia and granddaughter of Augustus, married Germanicus in AD 5 and accompanied him on campaign, which was itself unconventional. During the Rhine mutiny of 14 she left the camp with the infant Gaius, shaming the soldiers; in 15 she stood at the Rhine bridge to prevent its destruction and welcomed the retreating troops with clothes and bandages, which Tiberius resented as usurping a commander's role. She went east with Germanicus in 17 and, after his death in 19, carried his ashes from Antioch to Brundisium and Rome, a procession that made her a symbol of loyalty. Convinced that Tiberius and Livia had caused her husband's death, she became the centre of a political faction promoting her sons Nero and Drusus as heirs. Her pride and temper, which Tacitus repeatedly notes, made her an easy target for Sejanus: in 26 she asked Tiberius for permission to remarry, which he refused, and at a dinner she refused to eat fruit he offered, fearing poison. After Livia's death in 29 Tiberius denounced her and Nero to the Senate. She was exiled to Pandateria, where a centurion beat her so badly that she lost an eye, and she starved herself to death on 18 October 33, the second anniversary of Sejanus's fall; Tiberius boasted that he had not strangled her. Nero had died on Pontia in 31 and Drusus was starved in a palace dungeon in 33. Caligula, her third son, brought her ashes and those of Nero to the Mausoleum of Augustus in 37; the inscribed urn base survives in the Capitoline Museums. Her daughter Agrippina the Younger became empress and mother of Nero. Tacitus's portrait, sympathetic but critical, emphasises her chastity, fertility and ambition. Modern scholars see her as an early example of a woman wielding influence through dynastic legitimacy and popular sympathy rather than formal position.

Lucius Aelius Sejanus was born at Volsinii in Etruria c. 20 BC, son of Lucius Seius Strabo, praetorian prefect under Augustus, and of a woman of senatorial family; he was adopted into the gens Aelia. He accompanied Gaius Caesar to the East and became joint prefect with his father in 14, sole prefect when Strabo became prefect of Egypt. Tacitus's famous portrait (Annals 4.1) describes him as physically tough, bold, secretive, a mixture of servility and arrogance, his ambition aimed at supreme power. In 23 he concentrated the praetorian cohorts in the Castra Praetoria on the Viminal, creating a formidable instrument. He won Tiberius's trust, especially after saving him in 26 when a grotto collapsed at Sperlonga. In 23, Drusus the Younger, who had struck him, died, poisoned according to later testimony by Sejanus and Drusus's wife Livilla, whom he had seduced. In 25 he asked to marry Livilla and Tiberius refused, warning of senatorial resentment. After Tiberius withdrew to Capri in 26, Sejanus controlled access and correspondence, and engineered the prosecution of the friends of Agrippina and the exile of Agrippina and her son Nero (29) and imprisonment of Drusus (30). Statues of him were set up beside the emperor's, his birthday was celebrated, and he held the consulship of 31 with Tiberius. He received proconsular imperium and seemed about to receive tribunician power when Tiberius, warned (according to Josephus) by Antonia, turned on him. On 18 October 31 he was arrested in the Senate on the reading of Tiberius's letter and executed the same day. His body was abused for three days and thrown into the Tiber, and his children were executed. Juvenal used his fall as the classic example of the vanity of ambition. Modern historians debate whether he plotted a coup or was simply destroyed by Tiberius's suspicion; his career demonstrated the potential of the praetorian prefecture, which several later prefects exploited.

Gaius Julius Caesar Germanicus, born on 31 August 12 at Antium, son of Germanicus and Agrippina the Elder, grew up in military camps on the Rhine, where soldiers nicknamed him Caligula ("Little Boot") for his miniature uniform. He survived the destruction of his mother and brothers by obsequiousness, lived on Capri with Tiberius from 31 and was named co-heir with Tiberius Gemellus. Acclaimed emperor in March 37 aged 24, he was hugely popular at first: he burned the records of treason trials, recalled exiles, published the imperial accounts and restored elections. In October 37 he fell gravely ill, and afterwards, according to the sources, his behaviour changed. He had Gemellus and Macro killed, lived openly with his sisters (with whom incest was alleged), deified Drusilla on her death in 38, and squandered Tiberius's surplus on spectacles, building projects such as the bridge at Baiae, the Nemi ships, the Vatican circus and the aqueducts. In 39 he revived treason trials, broke with the Senate, and after uncovering the conspiracy of Gaetulicus and Lepidus, exiled his sisters Agrippina and Julia Livilla. His northern expedition of 39-40 ended with soldiers collecting seashells on the Channel coast as "spoils of the Ocean". He demanded worship as a living god, ordered his statue placed in the Jerusalem Temple, had Ptolemy of Mauretania killed and annexed his kingdom. He was murdered by praetorian officers on 24 January 41. The extreme anecdotes of the sources, including the plan to make his horse Incitatus consul, are now often read as distortions of a young autocrat's sarcasm and contempt for the Senate (Barrett, Winterling) rather than evidence of insanity, although Suetonius and Philo describe mental instability. Philo, who met him, offers an eyewitness view of his mockery. Seneca, who survived his hostility, depicts him as the archetype of cruelty. His reign showed how completely the Principate depended on the character of its holder.
set.debate: Madness (ancient tradition) or rational if brutal autocracy distorted by hostile sources (Winterling).

set.detail: Tiberius Claudius Nero Germanicus, born at Lugdunum on 1 August 10 BC, son of Drusus the Elder and Antonia, suffered from a physical disability, possibly cerebral palsy, that caused a limp, tremor and stammer, and was kept from public life by Augustus and Tiberius; his mother called him a "monster of a man". He devoted himself to scholarship, writing histories of the Etruscans (20 books) and Carthaginians (8 books) in Greek and a history of Rome from 44 BC, encouraged by Livy, and a defence of Cicero. Caligula made him consul in 37 but treated him with contempt. Made emperor by the praetorians in 41, he proved an active and innovative ruler. He conquered southern Britain (43), annexed Mauretania, Lycia, Thrace and Judaea, built the harbour at Portus, the Aqua Claudia and Anio Novus and the drainage tunnel of the Fucine Lake, revived the censorship (47-48) and admitted Gallic nobles to the Senate, defending the decision in a speech preserved on the Lyon tablet. He extended citizenship generously, regulated the treatment of slaves, devoted enormous time to judging cases in person, and developed the central bureaucracy staffed by freedmen such as Narcissus, Pallas, Callistus and Polybius. These features, together with his reliance on his wives, made him the butt of senatorial hostility: Seneca's Apocolocyntosis, Suetonius and Tacitus depict him as absent-minded, pedantic and dominated by women and freedmen. His third wife Messalina was executed in 48 after her bigamous marriage to Gaius Silius, and his fourth, his niece Agrippina, induced him to adopt her son Nero in preference to Britannicus. He executed 35 senators and over 300 knights. He died in October 54, probably poisoned by Agrippina, and was deified. Modern historians (Momigliano, Levick, Osgood) have rehabilitated him as a capable administrator whose reign consolidated the imperial system, and Robert Graves's novels made him a popular figure.

Valeria Messalina, born c. 17-20, great-granddaughter of Octavia through both parents, married her cousin Claudius around 38 and bore him Claudia Octavia and Britannicus (41). As empress she was immensely influential, controlling access to Claudius together with the freedmen, and she used that power to eliminate rivals: Julia Livilla and Seneca (41), Appius Silanus (42), Julia daughter of Drusus (43), Poppaea Sabina the Elder and Valerius Asiaticus (47), the last of whom she reputedly destroyed to get his gardens. Ancient writers, above all Juvenal (Satire 6), Pliny the Elder, Tacitus and Dio, portray her as insatiable: Juvenal has her slipping out of the palace at night to work in a brothel under the name Lycisca, Pliny claims she competed with a prostitute to see who could have more partners in a night. In 48, while Claudius was at Ostia, she went through a formal marriage ceremony with the consul designate Gaius Silius, with witnesses, a dowry and a feast. The freedman Narcissus, fearing a coup, persuaded Claudius through his concubines that Silius aimed at the throne; Silius and many others were executed. Messalina, waiting in the Gardens of Lucullus, was killed on Narcissus's orders before Claudius, who was said to be softening, could see her; told of her death at dinner, he asked for more wine. The Senate ordered her name removed from monuments. The marriage to Silius remains puzzling: modern historians suggest it was a genuine conspiracy to replace Claudius with Silius as regent for Britannicus, either initiated by Messalina to protect her position as Claudius aged and Agrippina rose, or a plot by Narcissus to destroy her. Her sexual reputation, magnified by later satirists, is regarded with scepticism, as political charges against women typically took sexual form. Her fall opened the way for Agrippina's marriage to Claudius and Nero's succession.
set.debate: Whether the marriage to Silius was a coup attempt, a plot by Narcissus or a reckless affair.

set.detail: Julia Agrippina, born on 6 November 15 at Ara Ubiorum (later named Colonia Agrippinensis in her honour), daughter of Germanicus and Agrippina the Elder, married Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus in 28 and bore Lucius Domitius, the future Nero, in December 37. Under her brother Caligula she was honoured with her sisters, then exiled in 39 for involvement in the Lepidus conspiracy, and recalled by Claudius in 41. After Messalina's fall she married her uncle Claudius in 49, the Senate having changed the law forbidding marriage with a brother's daughter. She secured Nero's adoption (50) and marriage to Octavia (53), had Seneca recalled as his tutor and Burrus appointed praetorian prefect, and became the first living wife of an emperor to receive the title Augusta and to appear on coins. She received foreign envoys, sat on a tribunal before the standards when Caratacus was paraded, and had a colony founded in her name. She is accused of poisoning Claudius in 54 to secure Nero's succession. In the first year of Nero's reign she appeared on coins facing him, but her domination provoked resistance from Seneca, Burrus and Nero himself; the murder of Britannicus in 55 and her removal from the palace marked her decline. She was murdered on Nero's orders in 59 after the failed attempt with the collapsing boat. She wrote memoirs (commentarii), used by Tacitus and Pliny, which recounted her family's misfortunes. Tacitus describes her as possessing "masculine domination", seeking power for herself through men. Modern historians (Barrett, Ginsburg) emphasise that the hostile portrait reflects senatorial anxiety about female power, while acknowledging her skill and ruthlessness. She was the only woman to be daughter, sister, wife and mother of emperors. Her temple to Divus Claudius on the Caelian was completed later by Vespasian.

Nero Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, born Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus on 15 December 37 at Antium, became emperor at sixteen in October 54. The early reign, guided by Seneca and Burrus, was well regarded: the Senate's role was respected, Corbulo restored the position in Armenia and the treasury was managed carefully. After murdering Britannicus (55) and his mother Agrippina (59), Nero turned to his passions for the lyre, poetry, chariot racing and Greek culture, founding the Juvenalia and Neronia and performing in public, scandalising the aristocracy. Burrus's death in 62, Seneca's retirement and the rise of Tigellinus brought a harsher regime: he divorced and executed Octavia and married Poppaea Sabina, who died in 65, reportedly after he kicked her while pregnant. The Boudican revolt (60-61) and the defeat at Rhandeia (62) were followed by the compromise with Parthia that brought Tiridates to Rome for coronation (66). The Great Fire of 64, for which rumour blamed him and he blamed the Christians, was followed by his rebuilding of Rome with a new building code and the vast Domus Aurea, and by a coinage reform. The Pisonian conspiracy of 65 led to the deaths of Seneca, Lucan, Petronius and many others, and Corbulo was forced to suicide in 67. His tour of Greece (66-67), in which he competed in all the festivals and won 1,808 prizes, ended with the proclamation of Greek freedom at Corinth and the start of the Corinth canal. The revolts of Vindex and Galba in 68 found him unable to act, and he killed himself on 9 or 11 June 68. The senatorial tradition (Tacitus, Suetonius, Dio) made him the archetypal tyrant, and Christians identified him with the Antichrist, but his popularity with the urban plebs and in the Greek East lasted, as false Neros show. Modern scholars (Griffin, Champlin, Drinkwater) analyse him as a performer emperor whose behaviour, though often brutal, was more rational and populist than the sources admit.

Lucius Annaeus Seneca was born at Corduba c. 4 BC, son of the elder Seneca, the rhetorician, and brother of Gallio and of Mela, father of Lucan. Brought to Rome as a child, he studied rhetoric and Stoic and Pythagorean philosophy (with Attalus and Sotion), spent time in Egypt for his health and entered the Senate under Tiberius. A brilliant orator, he aroused Caligula's jealousy and in 41 was exiled to Corsica on Messalina's charge of adultery with Julia Livilla. Recalled in 49 by Agrippina to tutor her son, he became, with the prefect Burrus, the guiding minister of Nero's early reign, writing his speeches, including the accession speech and the eulogy of Claudius, while privately composing the satire Apocolocyntosis and the treatise De Clementia. He was implicated, at least in the cover-up, in the murder of Agrippina in 59. After Burrus's death in 62 he tried to retire and offered Nero his fortune, estimated at 300 million sesterces, much of it from loans that Dio blamed for provoking the Boudican revolt. In retirement he wrote the Natural Questions and the Moral Letters to Lucilius. Accused of involvement in the Pisonian conspiracy in 65, he was ordered to die; Tacitus describes his long death, in which he opened his veins, took hemlock and finally suffocated in a hot bath, dictating to secretaries and comforting his wife Paulina, who tried to die with him. His works include dialogues on anger, the brevity of life, providence, tranquillity and constancy, consolations, De Beneficiis and nine tragedies (Medea, Phaedra, Thyestes, Oedipus and others) that shaped Renaissance drama. The contrast between his teaching and his wealth and complicity was attacked in his lifetime by Suillius Rufus and has shaped his reputation since. Medieval Christians even forged a correspondence between him and Paul.

Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo, son of a senator of the same name, was consul suffect probably in 39; his half-sister Milonia Caesonia was Caligula's wife. Appointed by Claudius to Lower Germany in 47, he defeated the Chaucian pirate leader Gannascus, settled the Frisii and enforced strict discipline, making his soldiers dig a canal between the Rhine and the Meuse, but Claudius ordered him to withdraw behind the Rhine, prompting his remark "how fortunate the Roman generals of old were". After governing Asia, he was sent by Nero in 54 to command in Cappadocia and Galatia against Parthian control of Armenia. He spent years retraining the softened Syrian legions, wintering them in tents in the Armenian highlands with severe punishments, then in 58 took and burned Artaxata and in 59 Tigranocerta, installing Tigranes VI. When his successor Caesennius Paetus capitulated at Rhandeia (62), Corbulo, now governor of Syria, was given an extraordinary maius imperium over the East, invaded Armenia again and in 63 negotiated the settlement of Rhandeia, by which Tiridates received the Armenian crown from Nero in Rome in 66. Corbulo was the most famous general of his age, a tall, imposing figure who wrote memoirs used by Tacitus and Pliny. In 67 Nero summoned him to Greece, and at Cenchreae, on landing, he received the order to die. He stabbed himself, saying "I deserved it" (axios). The reason is unclear: his son-in-law Annius Vinicianus had been involved in a conspiracy at Beneventum in 66. His daughter Domitia Longina married Domitian, and the Flavians honoured his memory. Tacitus admires his discipline but notes his vanity and his manipulation of reports to enhance his reputation at others' expense, especially Paetus's. Modern historians see his career as an example of the limits imposed on great generals by imperial suspicion.

Arminius, born c. 18 or 17 BC, son of the Cheruscan noble Segimer, served with his brother Flavus as an officer of Cheruscan auxiliaries in the Roman army, probably in the Illyrian war, and received citizenship and equestrian rank; his Germanic name is unknown (the identification with "Hermann" is a sixteenth-century invention). Trusted by Varus, he organised a coalition of the Cherusci, Bructeri, Marsi and Chatti, and in September AD 9 lured Varus's army into an ambush and destroyed three legions. He sent Varus's head to Maroboduus of the Marcomanni, inviting him to join the war, but Maroboduus sent it on to Augustus. He had abducted and married Thusnelda, daughter of the pro-Roman Segestes, who opposed him; in 15 Segestes handed her over to Germanicus while she was pregnant, and she and her son Thumelicus walked in Germanicus's triumph in 17. Arminius fought Germanicus in 15-16, nearly destroying Caecina's army at the pontes longi and fighting at Idistaviso and the Angrivarian wall, where he was defeated but escaped, his face smeared with his own blood to avoid recognition. Tacitus records a dialogue across the Weser between Arminius and his loyal brother Flavus, each denouncing the other in Latin and German. In 17 he defeated Maroboduus, whose kingdom collapsed, but his own growing power provoked fears that he aimed at kingship, and in 21 he was murdered by his relatives. Tacitus (Annals 2.88) gives him an epitaph as "undoubtedly the liberator of Germany", who challenged Rome at the height of its power, undefeated in war, still sung of among the Germans. The Chattan chief Adgandestrius had offered to poison him, but Tiberius refused, saying Rome took vengeance openly. In the nineteenth century Arminius became the national hero of Germany, commemorated by the Hermannsdenkmal near Detmold (1875), and his symbolism was later exploited by German nationalism.

Boudica, wife of Prasutagus, client king of the Iceni of East Anglia, led the most dangerous revolt against Roman rule in Britain. When Prasutagus died around 60, leaving half his kingdom to Nero and half to his two daughters, in hope of protecting his family, the procurator Catus Decianus and centurions seized the kingdom, flogged Boudica and raped her daughters; Iceni nobles were stripped of their estates. Roman financiers, including Seneca according to Dio, called in loans, and the veterans of the colony at Camulodunum had driven the Trinovantes from their land and built a temple to Claudius regarded as a citadel of oppression. While the governor Suetonius Paullinus was attacking the Druid stronghold of Mona, the Iceni and Trinovantes rose, destroyed Camulodunum, where the last defenders held out in the temple for two days, defeated part of IX Hispana under Petillius Cerialis, and burned Londinium and Verulamium, killing according to Tacitus 70,000 people with torture and impalement. Destruction layers of burnt red clay and ash dated to this time have been found in all three towns. Paullinus, having abandoned Londinium as indefensible, defeated her army in a battle somewhere in the Midlands, and Boudica died by poison or illness. Dio describes her as very tall, with a harsh voice, a mass of tawny hair to her hips, a great golden torque and a multicoloured tunic and cloak, holding a spear, and gives her a speech invoking the goddess Andraste and releasing a hare for divination. Tacitus has her declare that it was customary for Britons to fight under women's leadership. The spelling Boudica (from a Celtic word for victory) is now preferred to the Renaissance form Boadicea. She became a national heroine in Victorian Britain, symbolised by Thomas Thornycroft's bronze group by Westminster Bridge (1902), and her story continues to be debated in terms of colonial exploitation and resistance.

Herod, born c. 73 BC, son of the Idumaean Antipater, who served the Hasmonean Hyrcanus II and Caesar, and the Nabataean Cypros, was appointed governor of Galilee in 47 BC, where he executed the bandit leader Hezekiah, and was declared king of Judaea by the Senate in 40 BC on Antony's and Octavian's initiative after the Parthian invasion installed Antigonus. He took Jerusalem with Roman help in 37 BC and ruled until his death in 4 BC. He married the Hasmonean princess Mariamme, whom he executed in 29 BC, and successfully switched allegiance from Antony to Octavian after Actium, receiving back territory Cleopatra had taken and more. He became one of the greatest builders of antiquity: the rebuilt Temple in Jerusalem with its vast platform (begun c. 20 BC), the fortress palaces of Masada, Herodium (where his tomb was found in 2007), Machaerus and the Antonia, the port city of Caesarea with its harbour Sebastos, Sebaste (Samaria) and benefactions abroad, including endowments for the Olympic Games. He promoted Hellenistic culture and the imperial cult in his Gentile cities while respecting Jewish law in Jerusalem, a balancing act that earned suspicion from both sides. He maintained an efficient administration, relieved a famine in 25 BC with his own wealth, and protected diaspora Jews through his friendship with Agrippa. His later years were dominated by intrigue in his large family: he married ten wives and executed three of his sons, Alexander and Aristobulus (7 BC) and Antipater (4 BC), with Augustus's permission. His death, after a painful illness (possibly chronic kidney disease with Fournier's gangrene), was followed by revolt and the division of his kingdom among Archelaus, Antipas and Philip. Matthew's story of the massacre of the innocents at Bethlehem is not found in Josephus and is generally regarded as legendary. Josephus, drawing on Nicolaus of Damascus, is the main source. Modern historians stress his effectiveness as a Roman client king.
